qs.q: Find the determinant of $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&5\\6&7\end{bmatrix}$.
Find the determinant of $B=\begin{bmatrix}5&-1\\2&2\end{bmatrix}$.
Which statement about the determinant of a matrix is correct?

c.x: A matrix of the same size obtained from $A$
A number defined for every rectangular matrix
A real number assigned to a square matrix
A vector formed from the rows of the matrix

qs.e: The determinant is a single number (not a matrix) and it is defined only for square matrices.

qs.q: Using the $2\times2$ inverse formula $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(A)}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$, find the inverse of $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1\\5&3\end{bmatrix}$.
e: $\det(A)=ad-bc=(2)(3)-(1)(5)=6-5=1$, which is not zero, so $A$ is invertible.
Swap the diagonal entries and change the signs of the off-diagonal entries: $\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3&-1\\-5&2\end{bmatrix}$.

qs.q: Which relation between the cofactor $C_{32}$ and the minor $M_{32}$ is correct?
qs.e: $C_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}M_{ij}$. Here $i+j=3+2=5$ is odd, so the sign is $-$ (checkerboard position $(3,2)$), giving <mark>$C_{32}=-M_{32}$</mark>.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&3\\6&7&-1\\-3&1&4\end{bmatrix}$. Find the minor $M_{32}$.
e: Delete row 3 and column 2 of $A$. The remaining submatrix is $\begin{bmatrix}1&3\\6&-1\end{bmatrix}$.

qs.q: For the same matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&3\\6&7&-1\\-3&1&4\end{bmatrix}$, find the cofactor $C_{12}$.
e: Delete row 1 and column 2: the submatrix is $\begin{bmatrix}6&-1\\-3&4\end{bmatrix}$.
Position $(1,2)$ has sign $-$ in the checkerboard, so $C_{12}=-M_{12}=$ <mark>$-21$</mark>

qs.q: Evaluate $\det(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&3\\6&7&-1\\-3&1&4\end{bmatrix}$ by cofactor expansion along the <u>first row</u>.
For the same matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&-2&3\\6&7&-1\\-3&1&4\end{bmatrix}$, what value do you get when expanding $\det(A)$ along the <u>second row</u>?
e: $|A|=6(11)+7(13)+(-1)(5)=66+91-5=$ <mark>$152$</mark>, the same value as the first-row expansion.

qs.q: Find $\det(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0&-1\\3&1&2&2\\1&0&-2&1\\2&0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$.
e: Column 2 has only one non-zero entry ($a_{22}=1$), so expand along column 2. The sign of position $(2,2)$ is $+$.
In this $3\times3$ determinant, column 2 again has only one non-zero entry ($-2$ at position $(2,2)$, sign $+$): $=(-2)\begin{vmatrix}1&-1\\2&1\end{vmatrix}$.

qs.q: Find $\det(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&0&0\\-2&-4&3\\5&4&-2\end{bmatrix}$ by cofactor expansion along the first row.
e: The first row is $(3,0,0)$, so only the first term survives: $\det(A)=3\,C_{11}+0\cdot C_{12}+0\cdot C_{13}$.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&0&0\\-2&-4&3\\5&4&-2\end{bmatrix}$. In the cofactor expansion along the <u>second column</u>, what is the value of the term $a_{32}C_{32}$?
e: $a_{32}=4$. Delete row 3 and column 2: the submatrix is $\begin{bmatrix}3&0\\-2&3\end{bmatrix}$.
(Check: the other term is $a_{22}C_{22}=(-4)(+(-6))=24$, and $24-36=-12$, which agrees with the first-row expansion.)

qs.q: Find $\det(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0&0\\3&1&1&0\\1&0&-2&1\\2&0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$ using the row or column with the most zeros.
e: Row 1 has three zeros, so expand along it: $\det(A)=(1)\begin{vmatrix}1&1&0\\0&-2&1\\0&0&1\end{vmatrix}$ (sign of $(1,1)$ is $+$).
In the $3\times3$ determinant, column 1 has two zeros, so expand along it: $=(1)\begin{vmatrix}-2&1\\0&1\end{vmatrix}$.
$\det(A)=$ <mark>$-2$</mark> (the $3\times3$ matrix is upper triangular, so this equals $1\cdot(-2)\cdot1$).

qs.q: If $A$ is an $n\times n$ triangular matrix (upper triangular, lower triangular, or diagonal), then $\det(A)$ equals:
qs.e: Repeated cofactor expansion along the first column (or row) leaves only the diagonal entries, so $\det(A)=a_{11}a_{22}\cdots a_{nn}$, the product of the main diagonal entries.

qs.q: Find $\det(A)$ for the lower triangular matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0&0&0\\5&-1&0&0\\7&3&4&0\\1&9&6&3\end{bmatrix}$.
e: $A$ is lower triangular, so $\det(A)$ is the product of the main diagonal entries.

qs.q: Use the arrow technique to evaluate $\begin{vmatrix}1&2&3\\-4&5&6\\7&-8&9\end{vmatrix}$.
e: Recopy columns 1 and 2 to the right of the determinant.
Sum of the products along the rightward arrows: $(1)(5)(9)+(2)(6)(7)+(3)(-4)(-8)=45+84+96=225$.
Sum of the products along the leftward arrows: $(3)(5)(7)+(1)(6)(-8)+(2)(-4)(9)=105-48-72=-15$.

qs.q: The arrow (recopy-columns) technique for evaluating determinants works for which matrices?

c.x: Every square matrix, whatever its order
Square matrices of order two or three only
Only triangular matrices of any order
Square matrices of order at most four

qs.e: The arrow technique works <u>only</u> for $2\times2$ and $3\times3$ determinants. For $4\times4$ or larger use cofactor expansion (or row operations).

qs.q: Use the arrow technique to evaluate $\begin{vmatrix}-1&2&1\\0&2&-2\\1&4&0\end{vmatrix}$.
Find all values of $\mu$ for which $\begin{vmatrix}\mu-1&4\\1&\mu+2\end{vmatrix}=0$.
Find all values of $\mu$ for which $\begin{vmatrix}\mu-4&0&0\\0&\mu-1&3\\0&2&\mu\end{vmatrix}=0$.
e: Expand along the first row (only the first entry is non-zero): $(\mu-4)\begin{vmatrix}\mu-1&3\\2&\mu\end{vmatrix}=0$.

qs.q: Compute $\det(F)$ for $F=\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{bmatrix}$.
Evaluate $\det\begin{bmatrix}-1&4&2\\1&0&-3\\2&0&4\end{bmatrix}$.
e: Column 2 contains two zeros, so expand along column 2: only $a_{12}=4$ contributes.
(Check with the arrow technique: $[0-24+0]-[0+(-16)\cdot(-1)\cdot(-1)+0]$ gives the same value, $-24-16=-40$.)

qs.q: Find $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$.
e: The adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix: $\operatorname{adj}(A)=C^{T}=\begin{bmatrix}4&-2\\-3&1\end{bmatrix}$

qs.q: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{bmatrix}$, use $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(A)}\operatorname{adj}(A)$ to find the entry in row 2, column 1 of $A^{-1}$.
What is the adjoint of a square matrix $A$?

c.x: The transpose of the minor matrix
The inverse of the cofactor matrix
The transpose of the cofactor matrix

qs.e: If $C=[C_{ij}]$ is the matrix of cofactors of $A$, then <mark>$\operatorname{adj}(A)=C^{T}$</mark>. Minors alone (without the checkerboard signs) are <u>not</u> enough.

qs.q: Find $\det(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\3&6&5\\2&0&0\end{bmatrix}$.
e: Row 3 is $(2,0,0)$, so expand along row 3: $\det(A)=2\,C_{31}$.

qs.q: If the entries of one row of $A$ are multiplied by the corresponding cofactors of a <u>different</u> row and the products are added, the result is always:
e: This is the key fact behind the adjoint formula. Example: for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\3&6&5\\2&0&0\end{bmatrix}$ (with $C_{21}=0,\ C_{22}=0,\ C_{23}=4$), row 1 times the cofactors of row 2 gives $1(0)+2(0)+0(4)=0$.
The same holds for columns. The sum is <mark>$0$</mark>, while the same row with its <u>own</u> cofactors gives $\det(A)$.

qs.q: Find $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ for $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\3&6&5\\2&0&0\end{bmatrix}$.
To solve the system $x_1+2x_2+3x_3=9,\ 2x_1-x_2+x_3=8,\ 3x_1-x_3=3$ by matrix inversion, find $\det(A)$ of the coefficient matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\2&-1&1\\3&0&-1\end{bmatrix}$.
e: Expand along column 2, which has a zero ($a_{32}=0$): $\det(A)=2C_{12}+(-1)C_{22}+0\cdot C_{32}$.

qs.q: For $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\2&-1&1\\3&0&-1\end{bmatrix}$ the matrix of cofactors is $C=\begin{bmatrix}1&5&3\\2&-10&6\\5&5&-5\end{bmatrix}$. Which matrix is $\operatorname{adj}(A)$?
e: The adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix: rows of $C$ become columns.
Row 1 of $C$ $(1,5,3)$ becomes column 1; row 2 $(2,-10,6)$ becomes column 2; row 3 $(5,5,-5)$ becomes column 3.

qs.q: Solve $x_1+2x_2+3x_3=9,\ 2x_1-x_2+x_3=8,\ 3x_1-x_3=3$ using $X=A^{-1}b$, where $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{20}\begin{bmatrix}1&2&5\\5&-10&5\\3&6&-5\end{bmatrix}$ and $b=\begin{bmatrix}9\\8\\3\end{bmatrix}$.
e: Check in the equations: $2-2+9=9$, $4+1+3=8$, $6-3=3$. All correct.

qs.q: Use Cramer's rule for the system $x_1+2x_2+3x_3=9,\ 2x_1-x_2+x_3=8,\ 3x_1-x_3=3$ (here $\det(A)=20$). Find $x_1$, where $A_1=\begin{bmatrix}9&2&3\\8&-1&1\\3&0&-1\end{bmatrix}$.
e: $A_1$ is $A$ with column 1 replaced by $b$. Expand $\det(A_1)$ along column 2 (it contains a zero).

qs.q: In the same system (with $\det(A)=20$), find $x_2$ using $A_2=\begin{bmatrix}1&9&3\\2&8&1\\3&3&-1\end{bmatrix}$.
e: $A_2$ is $A$ with column 2 replaced by $b$. Expand along row 1.

qs.q: In the same system (with $\det(A)=20$), find $x_3$ using $A_3=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&9\\2&-1&8\\3&0&3\end{bmatrix}$.
e: $A_3$ is $A$ with column 3 replaced by $b$. Expand along column 2 (it contains a zero).

qs.q: Use Cramer's rule to solve $x_1-x_2=4,\ x_1+x_2=2$.
Use Cramer's rule to solve $2x+y=5,\ x-y=1$. What is $(x,y)$?
Cramer's rule can be applied to the system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ <u>only</u> when:
qs.e: Cramer's rule needs $n$ equations in $n$ unknowns (square $A$) <u>and</u> $\det(A)\neq0$, because $x_j=\frac{\det(A_j)}{\det(A)}$. Then the system has a unique solution.

qs.q: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&0&0\\1&4&0\\3&5&-5\end{bmatrix}$. Find $\det(A^{-1})$.
e: $A$ is lower triangular, so $\det(A)=(2)(4)(-5)=-40\neq0$ and $A$ is invertible.

qs.q: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ invertible matrix with $\det(A)=2$, then $A\cdot\operatorname{adj}(A)$ equals:
Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2&0\\3&6&5\\2&0&0\end{bmatrix}$, with $\det(A)=20$ and $C_{13}=-12,\ C_{31}=10$. What is the entry in row 3, column 1 of $A^{-1}$?
e: $A^{-1}=\frac{1}{\det(A)}\operatorname{adj}(A)$, and $\operatorname{adj}(A)$ is the <u>transpose</u> of the cofactor matrix.
